evidence.following_text: All Czech nouns have what is called gender. The gender of the noun is most important when you need to decide on the form of numbers, pronouns, and adjectives describing it. The words describing or determing the noun must change their form to match the noun’s gender. It also happens with verbs in the past tense. To match the noun’s gender, the other words have to either add an appropriate ending or changing an existing one. For example, ten bílý dům byl vs ta bílá kniha byla - that ‑masculine white ‑masculine house was ‑feminine vs. that ‑feminine white ‑feminine book was ‑feminine . English only has natural gender (used for people and male and female animals) but nouns in most other European languages have gender. French, Spanish and German are some of the best known. In Czech, just like in these other languages, you for the most part have to learn which words belong to what gender by heart. evidence.following_text: The word case refers to a set of endings that are used to indicate how words relate to one another. For instance, who does what to whom. In Czech, it is expressed through different endings. Nouns, pronouns, numerals and adjectives all use different case ending to express things like being an object (receiver) or a subject (initiator), or belonging to something. All prepositions also require that a noun has a case ending. Sometimes, the case ending tells you about whether you are somewhere or you are going somewhere. Sometimes a case ending helps link nouns together, e.g. if something belongs to something. In the English sentence, Petr has a son the relationship between Petr and his son is set by the fact that the word Petr precedes the verb and the word son follows it. headings.text: Special forms for talking to people: Rules for changing people's names when addressing them – another case?

evidence.following_text: The first thing to remember: in Czech, when you address someone you have to change the ending of their name. It really does make a lot of difference in establishing communication, even if you are speaking with the person in English. Expect that Czechs will change your name, too, when speaking to you in Czech. The second thing to remember: in polite conversation with someone older than you, or someone you don't know well always use their academic title rather than their name. Thus saying something like Mr. Doctor . Traditionally, this special form is considered a case called vocative . Czechs know it as the 5 th case (pátý pád). They all learn the rule as Pátým pádem oslovujeme (we use the fifth case to address).

headings.text: Informal, Endearing ways to address someone

evidence.following_text: Czechs sometimes use a special form of the first name to address people. This consists of the shortening of the name (unless the name is already short) and adding the ending -i for male or female names or occasionally -uš or -u for some female names. This is very informal and used only with the closest of friends in the context of endearment. Also, it does not work with surnames. In loving contexts, the -i is often lengthened to -í. Male names: Female names: Martin Marti Jana Jani Petr Petři Petra Petři, Petru, Petruš Karel Karli Veronika Veru Honza Honzi Jarmila Jaru, Jaruš Standa Standi Note: Not all names lend themselves to this form as well as others. Long male names ending in hard consonants such as Michal, Patrik or female names ending in consonants such as Karin. However, you will find that families may find other nicknames for people with these names to which this form can be added. Often, this form is only suitable to use within a family or a close group of friends.

evidence.following_text: Learning all the endings of Czech nouns may seem daunting. However, most of them are only used quite rarely. You will need to learn them eventually but, in the meantime, you can get very far with just six including when no ending is added, which is also important. They are: -y/i, -a, -u, - Ø, -ů, -e/-ě and are listed roughly in order of frequency and importance. As you can see, each of these endings can have multiple function and can be used different with different types of nouns. evidence.following_text: One that sometimes causes misunderstandings is the English conjunction that which actually serves a double purpose. Consider these English sentences: 1) This is the man that I saw. 2) a. He said that he would do it. / b. He doesn't know that he owes me money. These two are easily distinguished, and in Czech they require a different word. 1) in Czech, would be To je ten muž, kterého jsem viděl. while 2) will be a. Řekl, že to udělá. b. Neví, že mi dluží peníze. Který is really an adjective, and therefore it takes on the case of the noun in the main clause (in Czech grammars you will find it classified as a relative pronoun ). evidence.following_text: Contrary to popular belief, Czech word order is not completely free. In Czech, word order serves to show what you want to stress. The general rule is What you want to stress goes at the end of the sentence. For instance, take the simplest possible sentence Petr pije kolu. (Petr is drinking coke.) evidence.following_text: Czech prounciation is not particularly difficult. It is about as hard as it is to pronounce any language, if it does not happen to be the one you grew up with. This is because your muscles just find it hard to adjust to new things. It is true, however, that pronunciation is often the most difficult part for adult learners and adults very rarely achieve native-like accent. It is still important to practice pronunciation when learning Czech because Czech native speakers tend to value correct pronunciation over grammar when interacting with non-native speakers. A student of Czech will have an easier time trying to converse with natives speakers when getting the basics of pronunciation right.

evidence.following_text: There are a few peculiarities in Czech that tend to cause problems for English-speaking mouths. The most troublesome is the pronunciation of vowels . 1) no matter where they are in the word, Czech vowels never loose their full quality, and are always pronounced fully and unflaggingly. 2) each Czech vowel can be either short or long . Long vowels are exactly two times longer than their short brothers. It is very frequent that vowel length changes meaning of words significantly. For instance, děl a (cannons) is differentiated from děl á (s/he is working) only by the long á in the latter, and there are even more embarrassing examples. The length of vowels is completely independent on the stress . The stress is always on the first syllable in all Czech words. It is a very frequent that a long vowel occurs in an unstressed position as in dě l á . There are two diphthongs ou, au and eu that are pronounced fully, as well.

evidence.following_text: There are a few things that happen to individual sounds when put together. Especially consonants are vulnerable.
